question: Which type of trailer is most likely to get stuck on a raised railroad crossing due to low underneath clearance?
choice_a: A lowboy, car carrier, moving van, or possum-belly livestock trailer
choice_b: A tandem-axle tractor pulling a short trailer
choice_c: A flatbed trailer loaded with lumber
choice_d: A refrigerated trailer with a high roof
explanation: The manual specifically lists low slung units such as lowboy, car carrier, moving van, and possum-belly livestock trailers as trailers that can get stuck on raised crossings.

question: If your combination vehicle becomes stuck on railroad tracks, what should you do first?
choice_a: Try to free the vehicle by rocking it back and forth
choice_b: Get out of the vehicle and away from the tracks, then call 911 or the emergency number
choice_c: Uncouple the trailer and pull the tractor forward
choice_d: Stay in the vehicle and honk the horn continuously
explanation: The manual instructs drivers stuck on tracks to get out of the vehicle and away from the tracks, then call 911 or another emergency number, giving the crossing location using identifiable landmarks including the DOT number if posted.

question: What is the best and earliest way to recognize that a trailer has started to skid?
choice_a: Feeling the steering wheel vibrate
choice_b: Hearing the trailer brakes squeal
choice_c: Seeing it in your mirrors
choice_d: Noticing the tractor slow down
explanation: The manual states the earliest and best way to recognize a trailer skid is seeing it in your mirrors, and that you should check the mirrors any time you apply the brakes hard.

question: What is the correct action to stop a trailer skid once it begins?
choice_a: Apply the trailer hand brake to straighten out the rig
choice_b: Steer hard in the direction opposite the skid
choice_c: Accelerate to pull the trailer straight
choice_d: Release the brakes to let the trailer wheels regain traction
explanation: The manual says to release the brakes to get traction back; once the trailer wheels grip the road again, the trailer will start to follow the tractor and straighten out.

question: Why should you not use the trailer hand brake to try to straighten out a jackknifing trailer?
choice_a: The brakes on the trailer wheels caused the skid in the first place
choice_b: It is illegal to use the hand brake while moving
choice_c: It only works on tractors, not trailers
choice_d: It will disconnect the air lines
explanation: The manual explains that using the trailer hand brake to "straighten out the rig" is wrong because the trailer wheel brakes caused the skid in the first place.

question: What term describes the rear wheels of a vehicle following a different, shorter path than the front wheels when turning?
choice_a: Crack-the-whip
choice_b: Off-tracking
choice_c: Fishtailing
choice_d: Drift correction
explanation: The manual defines off-tracking (also called "cheating") as what happens when the rear wheels follow a different path than the front wheels going around a corner.

question: In a combination vehicle with more than one trailer, which set of wheels off-tracks the most?
choice_a: The steering axle of the tractor
choice_b: The rear wheels of the tractor
choice_c: The rear wheels of the last trailer
choice_d: The rear wheels of the first trailer
explanation: The manual states that if there is more than one trailer, the rear wheels of the last trailer will off-track the most.

question: When turning a corner, why should you keep the rear of your vehicle close to the curb while steering the front end wide?
choice_a: To avoid hitting street signs
choice_b: To reduce wear on the trailer tires
choice_c: To keep the fifth wheel aligned
choice_d: To prevent other drivers from passing you on the right
explanation: The manual advises keeping the rear of the vehicle close to the curb during a wide turn to stop other drivers from passing on the right.

question: When backing a trailer, which direction should you initially turn the top of the steering wheel to make the trailer go in the direction you want?
choice_a: The opposite direction from what you want the trailer to go
choice_b: The same direction you want the trailer to go
choice_c: It doesn't matter, either direction works
choice_d: Straight, then adjust only after the trailer moves
explanation: Unlike backing a car, straight truck, or bus, the manual states that when backing a trailer you turn the steering wheel in the opposite direction from the way you want the trailer to go.

question: If you must back a combination vehicle on a curved path, to which side should you back?
choice_a: The passenger's side, so you can see the mirror better
choice_b: The driver's side, so you can see
choice_c: Either side, since visibility is equal
choice_d: Whichever side has less traffic
explanation: The manual recommends backing to the driver's side on a curved path so the driver can see.

question: Before backing a trailer, what should you do to check your path?
choice_a: Rely solely on the backup camera
choice_b: Ask a passenger to stand behind the trailer
choice_c: Get out and walk around the vehicle to check clearance to the sides and overhead
choice_d: Sound the horn three times
explanation: Under "Look at Your Path," the manual instructs drivers to get out and walk around the vehicle, checking clearance to the sides and overhead before backing.

question: What should you do as soon as you notice the trailer drifting off the proper path while backing?
choice_a: Stop and re-inspect from outside before making any correction
choice_b: Continue backing at the same rate and correct only at the end
choice_c: Pull forward and start over from a different angle every time
choice_d: Turn the top of the steering wheel in the direction of the drift immediately
explanation: The manual's "Correct Drift Immediately" step says to correct drift as soon as you see it by turning the top of the steering wheel in the direction of the drift.

question: What is the trailer hand valve (also called the trolley valve or Johnson bar) supposed to be used for?
choice_a: Only to test the trailer brakes
choice_b: Normal driving braking
choice_c: Parking the trailer overnight
choice_d: Releasing the tractor protection valve
explanation: The manual states the trailer hand valve should be used only to test the trailer brakes, not for driving, due to the danger of causing a trailer skid.

question: Why should you never use the trailer hand valve for parking a trailer without spring brakes?
choice_a: It will trigger the ABS malfunction lamp
choice_b: All the air might leak out, unlocking the brakes
choice_c: It uses more fuel than the parking brake
choice_d: It disconnects the electrical cord automatically
explanation: The manual warns never to use the hand valve for parking because all the air might leak out, unlocking the brakes on trailers without spring brakes; wheel chocks should be used instead.

question: What is the purpose of the tractor protection valve?
choice_a: To supply extra air pressure to the fifth wheel
choice_b: To lock the trailer's landing gear in place
choice_c: To keep air in the tractor's brake system if the trailer breaks away or develops a bad leak
choice_d: To control the ABS malfunction lamp
explanation: The manual states the tractor protection valve keeps air in the tractor or truck brake system should the trailer break away or develop a bad leak.

question: Within what air pressure range will the tractor protection valve automatically close?
choice_a: 0 to 10 psi
choice_b: 60 to 80 psi
choice_c: 100 to 120 psi
choice_d: 20 to 45 psi
explanation: The manual states the tractor protection valve will close automatically if air pressure is low, in the range of 20 to 45 psi.

question: On newer vehicles, what does the red eight-sided "trailer air supply" knob do when pulled out?
choice_a: It shuts off air to the trailer and puts on the trailer emergency brakes
choice_b: It supplies more air to the trailer brakes for faster stops
choice_c: It releases the fifth wheel locking jaws
choice_d: It activates the ABS system
explanation: The manual explains you push the knob in to supply the trailer with air, and pull it out to shut the air off and apply the trailer emergency brakes.

question: What is the purpose of the service air-line (also called the control or signal line) on a combination vehicle?
choice_a: It supplies air to charge the trailer air tanks
choice_b: It carries air controlled by the foot brake or trailer hand brake to apply the trailer brakes
choice_c: It powers the ABS malfunction lamp
choice_d: It only operates the landing gear
explanation: The manual describes the service line as carrying air controlled by the foot brake or trailer hand brake, with pressure changing depending on how hard the brake is applied.

question: What are the two purposes of the emergency air-line (also called the supply line)?
choice_a: It powers the electrical cord and lights the ABS lamp
choice_b: It only inflates the tires and cools the brakes
choice_c: It supplies air to the trailer air tanks and controls the trailer emergency brakes
choice_d: It connects the glad hands and locks the fifth wheel
explanation: The manual states the emergency line first supplies air to the trailer air tanks, and second controls the emergency brakes on combination vehicles.

question: When connecting glad hands, at what angle should the couplers be pressed together before locking?
choice_a: 45 degrees
choice_b: 180 degrees
choice_c: 30 degrees
choice_d: 90 degrees
explanation: The manual instructs pressing the two seals together with the couplers at a 90 degree angle to each other, then turning the glad hand to join and lock the couplers.

question: What should you check or clean before connecting glad hand couplers?
choice_a: The couplers and rubber seals
choice_b: The tire pressure
choice_c: The trailer's registration sticker
choice_d: The fifth wheel grease level only
explanation: The manual says to clean the couplers and rubber seals before making a connection, since the rubber seal prevents air from escaping.

question: What happens if the emergency and service air-lines are crossed when coupling a trailer?
choice_a: The trailer brakes will apply with extra force
choice_b: Supply air goes to the service line instead of charging the trailer air tanks, so spring brakes may not release
choice_c: The ABS malfunction lamp will flash green
choice_d: Nothing changes; the lines are interchangeable
explanation: The manual warns that crossed air-lines send supply air to the service line instead of charging the trailer tanks, meaning air won't be available to release the trailer spring brakes.

question: What is the purpose of "dead end" or dummy couplers on a tractor?
choice_a: To increase air pressure in the system
choice_b: To test the ABS malfunction lamp
choice_c: To attach hoses when not in use and keep water and dirt out of the coupler and air-lines
choice_d: To lock the fifth wheel automatically
explanation: The manual explains dummy couplers hold the hoses when not attached to a trailer, preventing water and dirt from entering the coupler and air-lines.

question: According to the manual, what should you do with each trailer air tank's drain valve?
choice_a: Drain the tank only once a year
choice_b: Never open the drain valve unless there is a leak
choice_c: Leave it permanently open
choice_d: Drain each tank every day, even with automatic drains
explanation: The manual instructs draining each air tank every day; even with automatic drains that keep most moisture out, you should still open the drains to make sure.

question: When towing a single trailer with shut-off valves (cut-out cocks) at the back, what position should the valve at the back of the last trailer be in?
choice_a: Closed
choice_b: Open
choice_c: Halfway
choice_d: Removed entirely
explanation: The manual states that all shut-off valves must be open except the ones at the back of the last trailer, which must be closed.

topic: Trailer Service, Parking, and Emergency Brakes
question: Trailers and converter dollies built before what date are not required to have spring brakes?
explanation: The manual states converter dollies and trailers built before 1975 are not required to have spring brakes.
source_note: Section 6.2.8, Trailer Service, Parking and Emergency Brakes

topic: Trailer Service, Parking, and Emergency Brakes
question: Why is it important to use wheel chocks when parking a trailer without spring brakes?
choice_a: Chocks are required by law regardless of brake type
choice_b: Spring brakes cannot be tested without chocks
choice_c: The emergency brakes will hold only as long as there is air pressure in the trailer tank, which will eventually leak away
choice_d: Chocks prevent the ABS lamp from illuminating
explanation: The manual explains that on trailers without spring brakes, emergency brakes hold only as long as air pressure remains in the trailer tank; since air eventually leaks away, wheel chocks are necessary for safety when parking.
source_note: Section 6.2.8, Trailer Service, Parking and Emergency Brakes

question: Trailers and converter dollies built on or after what date are required to have ABS?
choice_a: January 1, 1995
choice_b: July 1, 2000
choice_c: January 1, 2005
choice_d: March 1, 1998
explanation: The manual states all trailers and converter dollies built on or after March 1, 1998, are required to have ABS.
source_note: Section 6.3.1, Trailers Required to Have ABS

question: Where is the ABS malfunction lamp typically located on a trailer equipped with ABS?
choice_a: Yellow lamp on the left side, either front or rear corner
choice_b: On the dashboard of the tractor
choice_c: On the rear bumper, colored red
choice_d: Inside the cab near the air supply knob
explanation: The manual states trailers will have yellow ABS malfunction lamps on the left side, either on the front or rear corner.
source_note: Section 6.3.1, Trailers Required to Have ABS

question: If only the trailer has ABS and you start to lose steering control or begin a tractor jackknife, what should you do?
choice_a: Apply the trailer hand valve immediately
choice_b: Let up on the brakes, if you can safely do so, until you gain control
choice_c: Accelerate to regain traction
choice_d: Shift into a lower gear and continue braking hard
explanation: The manual advises that when only the trailer has ABS, if you lose steering control or start a tractor jackknife, you should let up on the brakes if you can safely do so until you gain control.

question: According to the manual, does ABS necessarily shorten your stopping distance?
choice_a: Yes, it always shortens stopping distance significantly
choice_b: Yes, but only on wet pavement
choice_c: No, but it helps you keep the vehicle under control during hard braking
choice_d: No, ABS has no effect on braking at all
explanation: The manual states ABS does not necessarily shorten your stopping distance, but it does help you keep the vehicle under control during hard braking.

question: During the fifth wheel inspection before coupling, which way should the fifth wheel be tilted?
choice_a: Tilted up toward the front of the tractor
choice_b: Perfectly level
choice_c: Tilted to the left side
choice_d: Tilted down toward the rear of the tractor
explanation: The manual's Step 1 fifth wheel inspection checklist specifies the wheel should be tilted down toward the rear of the tractor for proper coupling position.

question: When positioning the tractor to back under the trailer, why should you never back under it at an angle?
choice_a: You might push the trailer sideways and break the landing gear
choice_b: It could damage the ABS sensor wiring
choice_c: It voids the trailer's warranty
choice_d: It causes the tractor protection valve to close
explanation: The manual's Step 3 warns never to back under the trailer at an angle because you might push the trailer sideways and break the landing gear.

question: What could happen if the trailer is too high when the tractor backs under it for coupling?
choice_a: The kingpin will bend automatically
choice_b: The trailer may not couple correctly
choice_c: The glad hands will disconnect
choice_d: The ABS lamp will turn off
explanation: The manual's Step 6 explains that if the trailer is too high, it may not couple correctly (while if too low, the tractor may strike and damage the trailer nose).

question: After connecting air-lines and supplying air to the trailer, how do you check for a proper trailer brake connection before starting the engine?
choice_a: Drive forward slowly and listen for squealing
choice_b: Check the fuel gauge for a sudden drop
choice_c: Shut the engine off, apply and release the trailer brakes, and listen for the sound of brakes applying and air escaping when released
choice_d: Rely only on the dashboard air pressure gauge
explanation: The manual's Step 8 instructs shutting the engine off so you can hear the brakes, then applying and releasing the trailer brakes to listen for the sound of the brakes moving and air escaping.
source_note: Section 6.4.1, Step 8 Supply Air to Trailer

question: How do you check that the coupling connection is secure after backing under the trailer (Step 11)?
choice_a: Drive at highway speed and check the mirrors
choice_b: Disconnect the air-lines and reconnect them
choice_c: Honk the horn and wait for a response
choice_d: Raise the trailer landing gear slightly off the ground and pull the tractor gently forward while the trailer brakes are locked
explanation: The manual's Step 11 says to raise the trailer landing gear slightly off the ground, then pull the tractor gently forward while the trailer brakes are still locked to check that the trailer is locked onto the tractor.
source_note: Section 6.4.1, Step 11 Check Connection for Security

question: When visually inspecting the coupling (Step 13), what does it mean if there is visible space between the upper and lower fifth wheel?
choice_a: Something is wrong; the kingpin may be on top of the closed fifth wheel jaws and the trailer could come loose easily
choice_b: This is normal and expected
choice_c: It means the fifth wheel needs more grease only
choice_d: It indicates the air pressure is too high
explanation: The manual's Step 13 warns that space between the upper and lower fifth wheel means something is wrong, since the kingpin may be sitting on top of the closed jaws rather than locked in, making the trailer come loose easily.

question: Why should you never drive with the trailer's landing gear only part way up?
choice_a: It reduces fuel economy
choice_b: It may catch on railroad tracks or other things
choice_c: It triggers the ABS malfunction lamp
choice_d: It prevents the tractor protection valve from closing
explanation: The manual's Step 15 warns never to drive with the landing gear only part way up, as it may catch on railroad tracks or other obstacles.
source_note: Section 6.4.1, Step 15 Raise Front Trailer Supports (Landing Gear)

question: Before backing up to ease pressure on the fifth wheel's locking jaws during uncoupling, what should you first do to the trailer's air supply?
choice_a: Push the air supply knob in to add more air
choice_b: Disconnect the electrical cord
choice_c: Shut off the trailer air supply to lock the trailer brakes
choice_d: Open the emergency line shut-off valve at the rear trailer
explanation: The manual's Step 2 for uncoupling says to shut off trailer air supply to lock trailer brakes, then ease pressure on the fifth wheel locking jaws by backing up gently.
source_note: Section 6.4.2, Step 2 Ease Pressure on Locking Jaws

question: When uncoupling a loaded trailer, why should you turn the landing gear crank a few extra turns in low gear after it makes firm contact with the ground?
choice_a: To lift the trailer completely off the fifth wheel
choice_b: To test the ABS system
choice_c: To disconnect the kingpin automatically
choice_d: To lift some weight off the tractor, making it easier to unlatch the fifth wheel and couple next time
explanation: The manual's Step 4 explains that for a loaded trailer, extra crank turns lift some weight off the tractor (without lifting the trailer off the fifth wheel), which makes it easier to unlatch the fifth wheel and easier to couple next time.
source_note: Section 6.4.2, Step 4 Lower the Landing Gear

question: When disconnecting the electrical cable during uncoupling, how should you hang it and why?
choice_a: With the plug down, to prevent moisture from entering it
choice_b: Coiled on the ground to avoid stretching
choice_c: Over the fuel tank to keep it visible
choice_d: Wrapped tightly around the air-lines
explanation: The manual's Step 5 instructs hanging the electrical cable with the plug down to prevent moisture from entering it.
source_note: Section 6.4.2, Step 5 Disconnect Air-lines and Electrical Cable

question: After unlocking the fifth wheel and pulling the tractor partially clear of the trailer, why should you stop with the tractor frame still under the trailer?
choice_a: To make it easier to reconnect the air lines
choice_b: To prevent the trailer from falling to the ground if the landing gear should collapse or sink
choice_c: To keep the ABS lamp illuminated
choice_d: To allow the parking brake to reset
explanation: The manual's Step 7 explains stopping with the tractor frame under the trailer prevents the trailer from falling to the ground if the landing gear collapses or sinks.
source_note: Section 6.4.2, Step 7 Pull Tractor Partially Clear of Trailer

question: When testing that air flows to all trailers during a brake check, what should you do at the emergency line shut-off valve at the rear of the last trailer?
choice_a: Leave it closed the entire time
choice_b: Remove it completely for the test
choice_c: Open it and listen for air escaping to confirm the system is charged, then close it
choice_d: Only test it with the engine running at full throttle
explanation: The manual instructs opening the emergency line shut-off valve at the rear of the last trailer; hearing air escaping shows the entire system is charged, after which you close the valve.
source_note: Section 6.5.2, Check That Air Flows to All Trailers

question: How do you test the tractor protection valve during a combination vehicle brake check?
choice_a: Disconnect the emergency line and count the seconds until brakes lock
choice_b: Drive at highway speed and slam the brakes
choice_c: Check only the dashboard warning light without touching the pedal
choice_d: Charge the system, push the air supply knob in, shut off the engine, and step on and off the brake pedal to reduce air pressure until the knob pops out
explanation: The manual describes charging the air-brake system, pushing the air supply knob in, shutting off the engine, then stepping on and off the brake pedal repeatedly to reduce tank pressure; the trailer air supply control should pop out within the manufacturer's specified range (usually 20-45 psi).

question: How do you test the trailer service brakes as part of a combination vehicle brake check?
choice_a: Check for normal air pressure, release the parking brakes, move forward slowly, and apply the trailer brakes with the hand control to feel them come on
choice_b: Apply the parking brake and check for smoke
choice_c: Only inspect the brake pads visually
choice_d: Disconnect the glad hands and listen for air loss
explanation: The manual's "Test Trailer Service Brakes" procedure has you check for normal air pressure, release parking brakes, move the vehicle forward slowly, and apply the trolley valve to feel the brakes engage, confirming they are connected and working.
